title: Chapter 53: The Net Closes, Part 4 of 5: Back for Him
html:
She could not go back the way she had come. The way she had come was on fire.
She knew it the moment she saw the light in the tunnel. The hay at the far end, by the mast, where the gap in the stacks was, was burning already. She could hear it now. A low steady roar, like a stove with the damper open, getting louder. And the smoke was coming. She could smell it coming. Thick and white and sweet, the smell of a summer meadow on fire, rolling down the tunnel toward her through the hay like water down a pipe.
She did not have long.
The lid.
Her grandfather's lid. She had not thought of it for years. She had shown it to the Captain, Oren, a week ago, on the Monday, when he asked if there was another way out of the hay room. There's the lid, Captain. My grandfather made it. For when the excise men came down the tunnel. A square of planks in the roof of the hay room, over the foot of the mattress, that lifted up. And on top of it, two bales of hay, set loose, on the very top of the stack. You pushed up the lid, and the bales tipped off, and you came out on top of the hay, under the sky.
She had never used it. Her grandfather had used it once, her father said, in the year of the great storm, and come out on top of the stack with a keg of brandy under each arm and a revenue man's pistol going off at his back, and jumped from the stack into the river.
She looked up at it.
The smoke was in the hay room now. A thin white curling layer of it, under the planks of the roof, getting thicker. The tin lamp on its nail had gone dim in it, a small orange smudge. The old lord was coughing. A small dry cough, like a cat's.
"Up," said Hessa Doon.
She got her shoulders under the lid. On her knees on the mattress, by his feet, with her head bent and her back against the planks of the roof. And she pushed.
It did not move.
It had not moved for forty years. The hay on top of it had settled, and packed, and frozen. She pushed again, with her whole back, with her legs under her, with everything. The way she pushed the pole into the river mud when the barge was stuck on a bar. The planks groaned. Something cracked.
And the lid went up.
Hay came down. A great choking rush of it, and cold air, and light. Gray-white daylight. And the bales tipped, and slid, and went off the top of the stack, and she was looking up at the sky through a square hole, with smoke going past it.
She got the old lord up.
She did not remember how. Afterward, if there had been an afterward, she would not have been able to say. She only knew that she had him. Blankets and all. Over her shoulder, the way you carry a sack. The way she had carried a boy of six out of the lock at Saltgate when she was nine. He weighed nothing. He weighed less than the boy had. His arms hung down her back and his head was against her neck and he was coughing, and she could feel his hand, on her back, through the blankets and her coat.
Tapping.
Four. Two. Nine. Three.
She went up through the square hole in the roof with him on her shoulder, standing on the mattress, then on the edge of the boards, then on nothing, pulling them both up by her arms with her elbows on the edge of the hole and her boots kicking at the hay. And came out on top of the stack.
And saw the Patient Grace burning.
The whole waist of the barge was on fire. All the stacks forward of her, from the mast to the bow. The tarpaulins had gone up first, and the hay under them, and the flames were standing up out of it now taller than the mast, orange and gold and white at the heart, with black smoke rolling off the top and going up and up into the still gray-white sky in a great leaning column. She could feel the heat of it on her face like a hand. The red sail on its yard was burning. The ropes were burning. The juniper on the tiller, at the stern, behind her, was still green.
The stack she was standing on was not burning yet. It was the last stack, at the stern, behind the hay room. But it was smoking. Smoke coming up out of it all round her feet, through the hay, in little white threads.
She looked down over the side.
The ice. Ten feet below. Gray-white, hard, with the black lane of the channel they had cut going away from the stern. And standing on the ice by the stern, in a ring, the gray coats. Nine of them. Young, red-faced, serious. Looking up at her. Not moving.
And in front of them, a little apart, the man in the round hat.
Vell looked up at her from the ice with his plain face. He did not have the lantern any more. He did not have the fishing rod. He was standing with his empty hands held out a little from his sides, palms up, the way a man stands under a tree when a child is up in it and might fall.
"Mrs. Doon," he said.
She could hardly hear him over the roar of the fire.
"Mrs. Doon. Hand him down. Please. To me. I'll take him." His voice was quite calm. "The stern will go in a minute. Hand him down."
Hessa Doon stood on the top of the last stack of the Patient Grace with the old lord over her shoulder and the fire behind her and the smoke coming up round her boots, and looked down at the man who had burned her barge.
And she thought: I could jump.
Off the other side. Onto the reed side. Where the ice was thick. Where Wat had gone. With him on her back. And run. Into the reeds, the way only Pask knew, toward the Mere, toward the boat at the Mere, three hours' walk, with an old man on her back and nine young men behind her and horses on the dyke.
She would not get a hundred yards. She knew that. She knew it the way she knew the river. They would catch her in the reeds, and they would take him off her back, and he would be on the ice in the cold with no blankets while they did it. And he was very old. And he was coughing.
Or she could stay up here, with him. On the stack. In the smoke. And the stern would go in a minute.
Or.
The tapping on her back had changed.
She felt it change. Through the blankets, through her coat. His thin hand, flat against her spine. Not four, two, nine, three any more.
Two.
Two.
Two.
Slow and steady. Over and over.
Two is hold, the Captain had said. That was the one the old lord had tapped, on the Monday, when the Captain went away to the city. Two, two, two. On the Captain's hand. Hold.
Hessa did not know what he meant. She did not know if he meant anything. He was an old man who did not know his own name, on her shoulder, in the smoke, tapping.
But she knew what hold meant. Every bargewoman knew what hold meant. It meant stay where you are. Don't let go. Keep her steady. Wait.
It meant live.
She knelt down on the top of the stack, in the smoke, and took him off her shoulder.
She did it gently. She laid him across her knees in his blankets, the way she laid Robin across her knees to change him. His face was gray and his eyes were open and he was looking up at her. Coughing. Holding the blue stone on his chest in his other hand, the way he held it every morning.
"I'm sorry, my lord," said Hessa Doon. "I promised you I'd take you home. Myself. I can't. Not today." She swallowed. Her throat was full of smoke. "I'll have to let somebody else."
The old lord looked up at her with his clear gray eyes.
And his lips moved.
She bent down. Close. With her ear to his mouth, over the roar of the fire.
And she heard it. One word. Very faint. Very dry. A breath with a shape in it.
"Hessa."
Her own name.
She had never told him her name. She had said it in front of him, on the barge, to Wat, to the girl, to the Captain, a hundred times a day for weeks. Hessa says. Ask Hessa. Hessa owes a goat. She had never once said it to him. And he had kept it. Somewhere. In some small room in the middle of all that hay.
Hessa Doon knelt on the top of the burning stack with the old lord's head in her lap and could not see anything at all.
Then she lifted him.
She lifted him over the edge of the stack, in his blankets, as gently as she had ever lifted anything, and leaned out over the side of the Patient Grace, as far as she could lean, with the fire at her back. And lowered him down. Down the black tarred side of the barge. Down to the ice. Into the waiting hands.
Vell took him.
He took him the way Wat had taken the baby. Slowly, and all at once, with both arms, against his chest. Blankets and all. He did not drop him. He did not jolt him. He held him, and stepped back from the side of the barge, and turned, and gave him to two of the gray coats behind him, who had a stretcher there on the ice, a plain canvas stretcher on two poles, and blankets on it, and a stone hot-water bottle wrapped in flannel. As if they had known. As if they had brought it all the way from the city on purpose.
They laid him on it.
Hessa watched them do it, kneeling at the edge of the stack, leaning over.
And as she watched, as they laid him down and drew the blankets up over him, she saw something fall.
A small bright thing. Blue. From the old lord's chest. From round his neck. It must have caught, she thought, on the edge of the stack, or on her coat, or on the side of the barge, as she lowered him. The fine gold chain had snapped. And the stone fell. She saw it fall. Not onto the ice. Back against the side of the barge, and onto the deck below her, at the stern, by the tiller, by the juniper. A tiny blue spark, going down into the smoke.
She opened her mouth to say something. To tell them. His stone. He's dropped his stone.
And behind her, with a sound like a tree falling in a storm, the mast went.
It had been burning at the foot for a long time. She had not seen it. She had been looking down. And now it went. Slowly at first. Leaning. The burning yard and the burning red sail swinging out from it in a great wheel of fire against the gray sky. And then faster. Down. Across the barge. Across the stern. Across the last stack, where Hessa Doon was kneeling at the edge with her arms still held out over the side, empty, the way you hold your arms out when you have just given somebody a child.
She did not see it come.
She was looking at the reeds.
At the place on the far side of the barge, the reed side, where the ice was thick, where the reeds had parted for a big red-bearded man with a baby in the crook of his good arm, and closed again behind him. Gold and gray. Millions of them. Frozen in. Standing very straight.
And she thought, the way you think things at the very end, quite clearly and quite simply and with no surprise at all:
Somebody will have to take Big Abel his goat.
And then the red sail came down over her like a blanket, and the Patient Grace took her home.
The Reeds
Wat Doon heard the mast go from three hundred yards off, in the reeds, with his son in his arm.
He knew the sound. He had been a sapper for four years. He had brought down a church tower once, at a town in the north whose name he had never learned, with powder in a tunnel under its foot, because the engineers said the enemy had a gun in the top of it. He knew the sound a great tall thing makes when it has been standing for a long time and stops. A long tearing creak, like a door the size of a house. And then a rush. And then the ground shaking.
The ice shook under his boots.
He stopped.
The reeds were all round him. Taller than he was, gold and gray, frozen in, so close together that he had been pushing through them with his bad shoulder, leaning into them, the way you push through a crowd. They closed over his head. He could not see the barge. He could not see anything but reeds, and the white sky in a narrow strip above them, and in the strip of sky, behind him, to the west, a great leaning column of black smoke going up and up.
And in the crook of his left arm, against his red-soaked shirt, his son.
Robin had stopped crying. He had stopped as soon as they went into the reeds. He was holding on to Wat's shirt with both fists, and his gray eyes were open, very wide, and he was looking up. Over Wat's shoulder. Back the way they had come. At the smoke.
Wat turned round.
He did not decide to. He just found that he had. He was standing in the reeds with his back to the way they were going and his face to the way they had come, and his feet had already taken one step.
"No," said Old Pask.
The old eel-man was in front of him, a few yards ahead, in the reeds, with his spear. He had stopped too. He had turned round too. He was looking at Wat with his little black eyes.
"No, Watkin Doon," he said. "She said go."
Wat did not answer.
He stood in the reeds and looked at the smoke. At the column of it, black at the bottom, going up. It had changed. It was thicker now, and lower, and spreading out at the bottom into a great flat cloud, the way smoke spreads when the thing that is burning has fallen down.
"She said go," said Old Pask again. "I heard her. Take my man and my boy across the fen to the Mere. She said she'd come after. She said she'd get him out of the hay and come after."
"She's not coming," said Wat.
He heard himself say it. His voice was very quiet.
Old Pask looked at him for a long time.
Then he looked at the baby.
"No," he said. "No, I don't think she is." He did not look away from Robin. "And if you go back, you'll not be coming either. And then there's nobody for him." He lifted his chin at the baby. "She knew that. That's why she gave him to you. Not to me. Not to the old lord. To you. Because you're the one with two legs and a back that can carry him to the Mere and a pair of hands to hold him after." A pause. "Well. One hand."
Wat looked down at his son.
Robin was still looking at the smoke. Over Wat's shoulder. With his mouth a little open, and his gray eyes very wide, and the light of the fire reflected in them, very small and far away, two little orange sparks.
He had his mother's eyes. Everybody said so. The same gray as the sky over the fen.
Wat stood there.
He stood there for a long time. Longer than a man should stand in the open, in the reeds, three hundred yards from nine men with torches. He did not care. He stood with his son in his arm and his back to the Mere and his face to the smoke, and his right arm hanging dead at his side, and the blood running down his back under his shirt, and he did not move.
And then, from far away, from the barge, from the fire, there came a sound.
Not the mast. Not the fire. Something else. Something he would never be sure of afterward. It might have been a beam giving way. It might have been the ice cracking in the heat. It might have been nothing at all, the wind in the reeds, except that there was no wind.
But it sounded to him like somebody shouting across a lock.
Loud and cracked and rough. The way she shouted. Across the black water between the gates at the Saltgate, to a lock-keeper who was being slow. Come on, then, Jory Hobday, are you going to open it or am I going to come over there and open it for you?
One word. That was all he heard. Or thought he heard.
Go.
Wat Doon turned round.
He turned his back on the smoke, and his face to the Mere, and put his head down, and pushed into the reeds with his bad shoulder after Old Pask, with his son held tight against his chest in the crook of his good arm.
And Robin, over his shoulder, went on looking back at the smoke until the reeds closed over it, and it was gone.
They did not get to the Mere. Wat's shoulder would not let them. A mile into the reeds, at the place where the old channel turned north, he went down on one knee on the ice with the baby still held tight against him and could not get up. And Old Pask stood over him for a moment, looking down, and then said, My hut, then. The long way. They'll not look in my hut. They think it's empty. Everybody thinks it's empty.
And they went round. The long way. Through the reeds, in a wide slow circle, all afternoon, with Wat on his feet again somehow and the baby asleep at last against his chest. To the little rise of ground no higher than a man's shoulder, and the turf hut with the sagging roof, and the cold hearth with no smoke.
Wat sat down on the heap of reeds against the turf wall, and held his son, and looked out of the low doorway at the column of smoke in the west, going gray now, and thinning.
He did not say anything. Wat never said much.
He sat there until it was gone.
